work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: The devil creates them, if they are created from the wound the devil inflicted on human nature as it was first made. Marriage is condemned if it is believed to contain something from which people deserving condemnation are born. Nor are all sins forgiven in baptism if some evil remains in baptized married couples, from which evil people are born. And how is God not unjust, if he forgives baptized people their own sins, yet condemns an infant because, when created by him, the infant unknowingly and unwillingly inherited other people’s sins—even from parents whose sins had been forgiven? Nor can virtue, whose opposite is understood to be vice, be thought capable of perfection: it is incredible that inborn faults could be destroyed. Indeed, these should no longer even be counted as faults. Someone who cannot be anything other than what they were created to be is not sinning.
translator_notes: Augustine first summarizes five accusations made by Julian’s side: that the doctrine makes the devil a creator, condemns marriage, denies complete baptismal forgiveness, makes God unjust, and destroys hope of perfection. The paragraph translated here is the direct quotation that follows that summary. “Vice” and “fault” translate the same family of Latin words; the argument turns on whether something inborn can be morally blameworthy.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: Those who are said to sin are not sinning at all, if, whoever created them, they must live according to the way they were created and cannot resist their own nature.
translator_notes: Augustine explicitly places this fragment in Book 1 of Julian’s To Turbantius.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: [He] works at nothing harder than making himself impossible to understand.
translator_notes: Julian’s accusation against Augustine. The grammatical person has been adjusted from Augustine’s framing; “[He]” identifies Augustine.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: [I do not] turn the filth of people’s conduct into an accusation against nature, or find comfort for its obscenities by insulting the apostles and all the saints.
[You] undermine the wall of modesty.
translator_notes: The first fragment concerns Julian’s claim that the speaker in Romans 7:19 is a person under the law, rather than Paul describing himself. The second is Julian’s accusation against Augustine; the supplied subject is bracketed. Augustine also reports, without setting out a separate full quotation, that Julian took comfort in displeasing a man who had not spared the apostles.

Review correction: the first fragment describes Julian’s own claim, since Augustine addresses Julian in the second person in the surrounding frame. The bracketed first person restores that perspective.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
kind: Arguments attributed to Julian’s side in Augustine’s recap
english: If God creates human beings, they cannot be born with any evil. If marriage is good, no evil comes from it. If all sins are forgiven in baptism, those born from people who have been born again cannot inherit original sin. If God is just, he cannot condemn parents’ sins in their children when he forgives the parents their own sins. If human nature is capable of perfect righteousness, it cannot have natural faults.
translator_notes: Augustine gives this as a closing statement of the five arguments advanced by Julian’s side. It overlaps the opening quotation at 2.1.2.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: [He would not] find anything to do or anywhere to turn, if pressed by the judges’ authority, if standing with me among learned people, if the trumpet of true reason and the weapons of the listeners standing around rang out.
[They] have lied to the crowd about us; they frighten people with the names “Caelestians” or “Pelagians,” and force agreement from people through fear.
All judges ought to be free from hatred, friendship, hostility, and anger.
translator_notes: Augustine interrupts the first fragment with his own comments. Those comments are omitted here, and the reported perspective is made explicit in brackets. The second fragment is Julian’s accusation against Augustine’s side. The third gives Julian’s standard for an impartial judge.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: [If he were] pressed by the judges’ authority, [he would] have nothing to do and nowhere to turn, since he could find no answer to my arguments.
Opinions should be weighed, not counted.
A crowd of blind people is no help in discovering anything.
[He] sets against me the helpless opinion of an ally and, as though panic-stricken, names his accomplices.
translator_notes: Augustine’s inserted comments and changes of grammatical person have been removed or marked with brackets. The first fragment repeats the challenge in 2.10.34. The imaginary reply “Far be it from me to call these men blind” is Augustine’s invention and is not included as Julian’s text.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: When judging a case, the noise of the crowds must be put aside. From every walk of life—whether priests, administrators, or governors—we should choose wisdom, rather than mere titles, for the examination of such questions. We should honor the few whom reason, learning, and independence raise above the rest.
[He promises] to conduct this case against us, one man on behalf of everyone.
It brings me greater glory before God to defend truth when it has been abandoned.
translator_notes: The second fragment is an accusation Julian makes against Augustine, which Augustine denies. The third describes Julian’s own role. The final quotation in Augustine’s section concerns something Pelagius said about Jerome, not a statement by Julian.

work: To Turbantius: fragments in Against Julian
english: “The common dregs of sedentary tradesmen,” “stirred up against us.”
“Soldiers”; “students in lecture halls”; “sailors, shopkeepers, fishmongers, cooks, butchers”; “young men who have broken away from the monks.”
“From a crowd of all sorts of clergy,” “because they cannot judge doctrines according to Aristotle’s categories.”
“We are denied an examination and a judgment by bishops.”
translator_notes: Augustine inserts these short fragments into a series of rhetorical questions of his own. They remain separate here to avoid inventing a continuous passage. Augustine identifies the first insult as Ciceronian. Its precise original setting is not established here; it is a classical echo, not a Bible allusion.
